reviews.review: Absolutely must-buy. It takes a usually yawnworthy genre (visual novel / interactive fiction) and a good underutilized setting and smashes them together. The result is a visual novel with none of its weaknesses - the player is constantly looking up new information, sifting through it, dragging the relevant bits to be uploaded to Orwell, and each of the 5 chapters seems to have a big pivot point that reacts to the player's choices. On top of all that, the mechanics are extremely well-woven into the narrative, giving a very strong simulation feel: each day you're waking up as a government employee tasked with sifting through endless infogarbage in order to tag & bag terrorists. It's wonderful.

Simply one of the best games I've played all year. As an IT security professional I always find portrayals of concepts like "internet" and "hacking" as pretty hard to swallow in both games and movies, but this games nails surprisingly well both the technical possibilities and the intricate moral dilemmas that arise with them. I've also been surprised by the quality of the script: even though it has some specific set of conclusions in mind, it's open ended enough to accomodate different nuances in the approach to the ethics of "privacy vs security in the age of surveillance".

The musical score deserve a special mention: it keeps you to the edge of the seat and enhances very well whenever you reveal certain pieces of critical information.

It's also worth a couple of replays to see how your actions can have different impacts, but be warned that it gets a bit tedious due to the fact that everything happens in real time and there's no way to speed up some parts (or at least, not obvious). I find the lack of checkpoints somewhat of a feature, since it gives weight to the consequences.

Again, kudos to the writing team for surprising some chilling aspects of the choices faced by all parties involved (and I want to keep this spoiler free, so I'll stop here).

My intention was to write this review after completing the fifth and final chapter after its release. Now that I've completed the game, I feel that I can give this game the review that it deserves. 

I was very, very surprised with how well this game was executed. I've never come across a game quite like this. Orwell is a game where you play as an investigator who is trying to discover the person behind a crime by ruffling through relevant internet posts as well as phone calls, emails, etc. You then send information you deem as relevant to your advisor, who then decides what to do with said information. As I was playing this game, I really felt the pressure on what kind of narrative I was showing to the government and the policeforce regarding the people I was investigating, which is why I believe this game is so brilliant. You really feel the need to think carefully about what things you send out because there is no taking back what you submit once it's out there, which I believe is one of the underlying messages of the game's story. 

I would liken this game to an interactive choose-your-own adventure. Regarding the gameplay, it does not involve much other than reading through files and articles, and clicking to drag data of your choice into the government's database. Certain pieces of information will unlock more articles and files for you to read through. That being said, while I was playing the game these simple mechanics actually helped me stay more immersed in the story. They were uncomplicated and helped my attention stay focused on my "job" and the impact I was having. If your idea of a good game involves more gameplay elements than this, I would not recommend it to you, but if you really enjoy a good story, then please consider giving this game a try. 

Where this game really thrives, I believe, is its attention to detail. The writing in this game is fantastic, as well as the music. The music is mainly ambient, but when you come across important information the music changes dramatically to match the feeling of what you have discovered. The writing paired with the music really kept me at the edge of my seat throughout each episode. I really enjoyed how versatile the writing was as well. The writers managed to create incredibly in-depth characters that each felt very real with their own motives and personalities. At times I felt obligated to protect these people or felt awful about info I might have uploaded about them if it turned out I was incorrect. Without spoiling anything, the writing really makes you think about how people generally show many different aspects of themselves to different people, and as the investigator you have to decipher which "mask" is the way that person really feels or thinks. 

Unfortunately for people who buy the game at this point, you will not be getting the weekly emails to report back to duty  because all five episodes have already been released. These emails really helped me stay immersed in the universe of the game and I really felt like I was reporting back to duty for a job, and I commend the developers for these small touches that added to my immersion in the game. Even though players who buy the game now have access to all episodes at once, I would really recommend taking a break of a day between each episode if you can. I really think it will help you stay immersed in the world. 

Honestly, if you enjoy dystopian stories like 1984 and want to experience an innovative way of playing, you will really enjoy this game. I hope that many people give this game a chance because it will really make you question government security and the things that you post publicly online. I'm going to keep an eye out for more games by these developers because I feel that they are really creating a new, innovative market and I am really excited to see what else they can bring to the gaming industry.

Orwell is a strange game to assess; having conducted several complete playthroughs I would cautiously reccommend the experience and certainly state that it is a well put together game, however, it is not without fault.

Before starting it is worth noting that your role in the game is very restricted, and meant to be, but this leads to frustrating situations wherein important information pertaining to context or inference is only privy to you, and you aren't allowed to present such information to Orwell, it's not your role. This creates a couple of game situations where you the player may be sensibly concluding one thing, but forced to provide information against your better judgement. This however seems intentional and part of the narrative so I don't judge the game poorly for it.

The game itself is politically minded without being pushy, allows for multiple playstyles at crucial moments, and certainly understands the value of consequence. Every choice made in the game is done relatively blindly, and all are irreversable, indeed it's the first thing you are warned of at the start. However with proper foresight and judgement, it is still possible to make correct and sensible decisions that result in an outcome that you desire.

The characters featured feel fleshed out, with rich characteristics and histories that add to a full feeling of an interwoven narrative, and with a plot that utilises these characters well, with innovative twists and character revelations that on a first playthrough are very satisfying.

Overall I would highly recommend this game to the fans of the genre, and to players in general, but I would state that subsequent playthroughs lose a lot of the initial spark, as a great deal of the game is built on tension and a well written narrative.

I just finished the last chapter of this game, and this is what I have to say:
Orwell is a very, very, very, VERY good game. An amazing game! Worth every penny I spent on it! It's nominated for The Game awards 2016, and toatally deserves it.
If you like invastigations, mysteries or investigating mysteries, if you like story-driven games or if yoy simply enjoy stalking people online, I HIGHLY recommend you give this game a try. You will not be disappointed!
The gameplay may feel to simple and the plot too linear at first (I know some people got that first impression), but please hear me out: This first impression is almost as far from the truth as it can get.

Now that you understand how good this game is, let's talk about what this game is ACTUALLY ABOUT :
So, in this game you are playing an investigator for the secret goverment program called "Orwell". Your job as an investigator is, well, to investigate.
How? Well, you have Orwell at your disposal! This program allows you to snoop around in other people's data that can be found online: public data and private data. data that was posted online willingly and data that noone knew even existed on the web. True, useful data and lots of half-truthes, misinterpreted information and straight-out lies. You need to find and gather this data, decide what's right and what's not, and report it.
Watch out, though, once a data chunk has been reported there's no going back - you must commit to whatever you belive the truth and face the consequences.
And believe me - THERE WILL BE CONSEQUENCES. Your decisions can and will affect the lives of tens if not hundreads of people. Maybe even the entire nation.
The story starts right after a bomb was set off in the middle of the city of "Bonton" in the nation called "The nation", (I know, such a good name for a country. Wanna guess what's the name of the prime minister's party? Yup - "The party".) killing many (can't remember the number) civilians and generally making everyone feel a bit worse about everything (What can you expect? A bomb just exploded in the middle of their city...) You start with barely any information - your only clue is that one person - a blue-haired woman - who's known to the police was spotted near the site of the attack just before the explosion.
Now you and your trusty advisor "Symes" must get to the bottom of this attack and try to prevent any future ones from occuring. On your way you will start to uncover many secrets - about your suspect (and the others that may or may not appear later on), about the mysterious group "Thought", and even about the entire nation, it's leaders, and Orwell itself.

Good luck ;)

[h1]“Big Brother is Watching You.” [/h1]
― George Orwell, 1984.

Orwell is a story driven puzzle (sort of?) game based around the idea of mass surveillance. The name is a reference to author George Orwell, famous for [i]1984[/i], a book detailing a man living in a country where "Big Brother" is always watching, where thought could be a crime, and the Party controlled what you were supposed to believe. 

[h1]“It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.”[/h1]
Set in [strike]America[/strike] [i][b]the Nation[/b][/i] in April, 2017, Orwell places you in the shoes of a newly hired Investigator, employees of the government whose jobs are to sift through and find information online to upload to Orwell, a new surveillance system currently being tested in the Nation. Your job begins after a bomb detonates in a busy city, prompting a search to uncover the group behind the attack. You become responsible for thwarting more attacks, unmasking the activist group Thought, and eventually determining the future of the Nation for years to come.

[h1]“He who controls the past controls the future. He who controls the present controls the past.”[/h1]
A terrifying piece of gameplay is the ability to write the narrative. A man comments in one place that he never wanted to harm anyone, while in another message, he expresses his satisfaction about recent events. To an extent, you are given the choice of deciding what Orwell and the Government learn about people.
Orwell is very obviously supposed to reference the situation beginning to develop in America right now, with whistleblower revelations revealing many of the activities conducted by some government departments. Surveillance is an increasingly relevant issue to today's world, and Orwell puts you on the other side of the issue.
One of the questions the game asks is whether or not the ends justify the means. You will trample over the privacy of many people, getting into their email accounts, bank accounts, computers, phones, and even forum accounts. Your methods are undoubtedly illegal, and you have multiple chances to ruin lives as you go.

[h1]“Until they became conscious they will never rebel, and until after they have rebelled they cannot become conscious.”[/h1]
(There isn't really a relevant 1984 quote about the part below.)

As for gameplay, you're staring at Orwell's GUI the whole time. There is a browser on the right, and profiles on the left. You gain information by dragging pieces of data (highlighted blue, or yellow if conflicting with other data) onto the relevant profiles, with your advisor giving his two cents from time to time. The game requires a lot of reading to fully understand the story. Orwell isn't a game you rush through. It's similar to a Telltale game in the way that gameplay<narrative. You will have to dig through websites, hack into computer desktops, and listen to conversations. 

The game took me about 4 hours to complete, but left me thinking about its topics for a long time after I logged out.

---

The biggest fault I have with Orwell is that there is no voice acting. Scenes where you listen in on calls could become so much more powerful with a decent voice actor or two to really put emotion into the characters.

I didn't like the fact tha Orwell was initially published on an episode base. I don't think it is the kind of game that calls for this overused format. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys policial or investigative simulations, as well as games where the choices of the player do matter.

I am thoroughly impressed by this game. It had a chilling ambiance that drew me in and immersed me. The fact my choices had an actual impact made it all the more fun. I don't believe I've been witnessed all the plot lines and possibilities, so i'm excited to replay the game at some point. In all honesty I did get a litte bored in the middle because I felt like everything had been revealed, but the ending in episode five made it worth it. That also could have been due to the choices I had made. Trying to reveal who was behind terrorist attack and save lives? Bruh you end up feeling like some sort of fucking scooby doo kid by looking at all the clues. I remember going through documents, going to past ones, trying to draw up conclusions based on timelines and shit, creating personas for people. The game is worth it my guy.

Bottom line up front: Orwell comes highly recommended as a visual novel relevant in our connected, surveillance-state times. Orwell is not a particularly difficult game. You merely act as the conscience for the eponymous automated evidence-gathering machine that potentially has access to everything in The Nation's network. You tell it what's relevant; it tells that to investigators responsible for actually acting as the long arm of the law. Of course, it's still basically in prototype so it's not necessarily that great at parsing relevant information. Drag and drop the relevant information. Think of it as a mystery simulator where you're a few steps removed from the evidence, and to piece things together you have to gather quite a lot of information from quite a few sources... say, from the desktop computer of someone who may only be tangentially related to the case at hand, or phone conversations between people of interest and total strangers. I say "total strangers" but, hey, they were talking to a person of interest, so doesn't that make them people of interest too? Let's get them introduced to Orwell, shall we? In the modern world where conspiracy theories like ECHELON and PRISM have turned out to be very real things made lawful through either everyday foreign spying or antiterrorism bills that authorize domestic surveillance, Orwell is a game about the flaws--and benefits--to such thinking. Are you able to stop terrorism (or, perhaps more accurately, are you willing to make the sacrifices necessary to do so)? Can you keep investigations limited despite your best intentions? Or do you just hoover up everything because there is no such thing as innocence, only degrees of guilt? And... in the end, how can it go so horribly, horribly wrong? Those in favor of a surveillance state will probably be somewhat annoyed with Orwell, but with a title like that they shouldn't be surprised. Those against surveillance states will appreciate it, though they may actually disapprove of the game's level-headed attitude towards such things: yes, it's a conspiracy, but it's a conspiracy of well-meaning people who are honestly(?) trying to make The Nation a better place by doing their jobs. It's a visual novel, so replayability is limited except for completionism and once you get a feel for how the writers like surprises, you can start to see some twists coming--or at least expect twists to happen--but this is a negligible criticism. Orwell is, at its core, about both freedom of thought and the inherent problem with surveillance and preventative enforcement: even with universal surveillance, information is neither perfect nor complete and errors will be made. The game occasionally forces these errors, which can be frustrating, but if you approach it as a choose-your-own-adventure story with a clever user interface these are forgivable.

Orwell has a great narrative. Stemming straight from its name it invokes suspicion and fear about Big Brother and the everlooming shadow of federal/national government. I greatly enjoy the point and click new-age software approach. Yet, not really that new-aged, since its not completely out of the realm of possibility that something like this exists. I find it challenging to decide if I truly have a say over the way the game goes, but it makes some decisions or lack thereof feel like that. Alot of ethical boundries are addressed in this game and sometimes it makes you rethink how secure you really are. For me, this game is the type of casual, but not-so-casual game I like to watch or play, such as Shenzhen I/O or Papers Please. I very much enjoyed the serious but totally accessible tone of the game aswell as the cell shading-esqe for certain parts of the game. I'm not a professional or anything but I sure know something fun and easy to engage in when I see it.

I bought thinking it was going to be like Papers, Please in a future setting but you don't really need to pay attention to details like you do in PP, the game basically spoon feeds you with all the necessary stuff you need to do. It could have been harder than this but I'm still going to suggest it because its concept and how it's been delivered is satisfactory. I hope they do a sequel and actually challenge the players.

This is a really clever, interesting game. Once the story got its hooks into me it wouldn't let go, and I ended up playing chapters 1-4 all at once. There is a lot of text, but it's not a slog by any means and even the parts that aren't directly relevant to your task for that day are still interesting to read for the worldbuilding and character building aspects. If you're a fan of point and click adventure games or visual novels, I reckon this will be right up your alley.
Very, very clever game - a partially on rails story that can deviate into various branches dependant on what information you choose to pass on. A steal for the price - can't wait for the 5th episode.
Absolutely a blast to play! I can't believe how fast I was sucked in to this game. Episode 5 needs to release right now!

This is a great experience, the game has a great story and is very immersive which allows you to dive more into the story, the sounds and the creativity is on point. I do recommend this game, it is worth the money spent on it. If you're into this type of games, you should try it. You got the demo, which is something awesome and rare to see.

Honestly, the most fun I've had in a game in a while.

The game is heavily based off of George Orwell's 1984, and by god do I love it. I even managed to get several friends into it as well. All in all, 9/10, mostly because it's episodical.

Welcome to the world of Intel.   
You want to gather, anaylze, and disseminate? you got it.
You want to feel as if you're only passing along the info and not acting on it? you got it. 
You want a story that's gonna blow your mind and leaving wanting more, only feeling slightly let down when you get the release date of the next chapter? You got it!!

This is well worth the money, just for the story alone. Grant it, it does hold your hand a bit, but not so much that you feel as if you don't have a choice in what to do with any of the information you gain. I honestly cannot say enough good things about this game without spoiling anything or repeating my words over and over again. Outstanding work, and I look forward to the next chapter.

This is not a game, it is a glimpse into our possible future... I can't wait for the next chapter. The story, the atmosphere is simply amazing.You don't always need fancy graphics for a game to be good. I think the artwork fits well.

You play as someone who works for the NSA but not the NSA for an imaginary country. It's a straight forward game, and honestly can't recommend it enough if you are someone, like me, who enjoys political story driven games. I just finished Episode 4 and god, please give me Episode 5 right now. The only downfall of the game is waiting for the next episode because you just want to know what happens next. The plot is great, all the different characters you 'interact' with are well thought out and well written. The little details, from the websites you explore to the music are fanastic. The art is beautifully done, and I really enjoy the style of everything. It's a great game for 10 bucks. 

Edit: After playing the last episode I would say this game in it's entirety is a blast to play with engaging storytelling right until the end.

The focus is on gameplay and decisions, rather than "ooo look a flashy button"-itus.

The plot is has a number of unexpected events in it, which make you think more about your choices. I like this.

The interface is good enough, although the later into the game you get the more information you have piled up to sort through.

Happy I played it, is certainly worth the money, would recommend.
I was instantly drawn into this game, and with all of its twists and turns it just keeps getting better. Highly recommended!
Extremely thrilling! Just played for 6 hours straight because I just couldn't stop and now I'm eagerly waiting for the final episode! Really cool idea, perfectly implemented, and a great story!

This is a really cool game. I know people are complaining about the way you upload data to Orwell (the important bits are already highlighted), but these people haven't come to learn the folly of their ways yet. If you just blindly upload any bit of data that is highlighted, there will be consequences. This is also supposed to present moral dilemma. Not only in the obvious Orwelian manner (is all this surveilance and government power "moral" or "right"?), but also from the standpoint of the people you are monitoring. It's not black and white. They aren't strictly bad guys. Will you bring damning evidence against a single mother who seems like maybe she just got caught up with a bad group of people? Will you hold someone's past crimes against them, drawing what may seem like a disproportionate response from authorities? 

TL;DR - Don't play the game to beat it. This is a scenic walk, not a foot race. 

Also, the devs seem pretty active. I posted an issue on the forums, and had a dev response within the hour pretty much. I bought this game, I regret nothing, and am eagerly waiting for day 5.
realy fun game playing this  made me feel like a real life hacker   i realy recommend buying this

Incredible. Smart. Educational. Reflective. 
Play this game. You'll know yourself and the world around you better afterwards.

You can feel the tension build while racing to connect the dots and prevent another terrorist attack...digging into the phone calls, texts, chats, emails, medical reports, and desktops of private individuals while monitoring social media in real time will do that to a person. A rather cool story, gameplay is unchallenging and not really the focus. The focus is a compelling interactive story where most of the choice is how much you do your job and how much of what info you upload to the Orwell system.

I really like this kind of game, its more interested in making you think a little and exploring its own themes than anything else, so if you liked 1984 and want to see an Orwellian take on the information era, then this is really worth playing.

An intriguing game experience. You are at the helm of an omnipresent surveillance system, analyzing different sets of data. Although the datasets are often very binary or exclusionary. But this in turn can lead to your decisions being important in the long run. It all happens from a web interface.

I would love even more if someone remade Sid Meier's Covert Action (1990), where you don't just collect data sets, but also try to analyze them for a bigger picture. But this is a very intriguing game, and it highlights a lot of the same problems we are facing in today's societies.

For some this game may be eye-opening. It addresses the modern, information-era issues in an interesting way.
Episodes 1-4 can grip you with the story, hopefully ep. 5 will keep up the good work. It took me a moment to get used to the art style but for me it is a good choice, it fits the game well.

Definitely worth a play.  It is short, you may only get one playthrough out of it, but it's a very well told story if you are at all into the big brother concept it portrays.  I eagerly await the 5th episode!

I had been watching this one for a few weeks now, and I'm glad I decided to purchase it.  Gameplay is sort of linear, and part of me wishes it didn't point out exactly what you needed to click on next as that mitigated the investigative feeling a little bit, though there are a few spots where you can decide which "truth" to go with, and I assume this changes the story around a bit. 

On the other hand, I quite like that the "hand-holding" present does keep the story moving and remove any dead searching and re-reading time that would be painfully present otherwise.

All in all, worth the purchase.   I can only hope the ending is worthy of the rest of the story.  I will update this if I remember after the 5th episode comes out!

To the devs, Great work so far!  Beautiful, easy to understand interface, well written story, and a few heart jump twists.
It's fun if you like this kind of thing. I also recommend Replica, which is like a more meta version of this.

I'll be honest, when I purchased Orwell I did so on a steam sale, as my expectations of this game were not high. I thought that this would be the game you "play for a few hours because you bought it and it's kind of OK, and maybe you'll finish it in a few months, but in reality you never will and every-single-time you see the game in the library you'll think "Oh, better finish that!" and then feel guilty for spending the money, but at least you got it on a sale!" kind of game. 

I did not expect to be sitting at the edge of my seat every Thursday for a new episode, grieving over the things that happen to the lives I'm invading and battling with my own morals and conscience half the time. Orwell, seriously, has become one of my top 5 favorites. As devoted fan of "Life is Strange", I didn't think Orwell would emotionally capture me the same way I felt in that game, but I'd say it has. You become familiar and interested in the lives you investigate, almost personalizing them to your own life and experiences in ways I didn't think were possible. 

Now for the Tl;dr: 

Pros 
[*] Amazing storyline - keeps you interested and captivated
[*] Unique format - I've never personally played a game like this before, and the fact it's 'you' controlling the information put into the computer system makes it feel that much more personalized. You start feeling like this is your actual job. 
[*] Choice based - although some of the storyline is somewhat linear, I have heard of different outcomes for different plots 
[*] Emotionally captivating - no spoilers, but you defiitely have your heartstrings tugged at least once or twice
[*] Has replay value - I'm honestly about to start over when I finish this storyline so see how my choices effect gameplay in the end. 

Cons
[*] The game highlights sections of information that is important to your investigation, and although this is helpful, sometimes I wish that we would [b]have[/b] to read the information and it wasn't highlighted until we asked for a "hint" on what information we needed. That may be too difficult to programme, and maybe some people would hate that format/idea, but I think it would add more value in terms of gameplay. 


Overall, this game is a solid 5/5 for me!

I'm loving this game at the moment.  You have to investigate the lives of suspects of a terrorist incident, you need to review all aspects of their lives, what they write online, their phone calls, text messages, their past, litterally everything, building a profile of their lives.  The best thing I like about it is how you choose to interpret the data you come across.  If you make a wrong assumption based on a single bit of imformation, it could change the way events play out, you could end up going for the wrong person, or fail to evacuate the wrong place when a bomb threat is found.

All in all, very imersive, great soundtrack, and new episodes coming out every week or so.  Awesome little game, and a great price to boot.
So far, this has been a very fun game that has an interesting way of telling a story and interacting with the world. I hope the developer makes new stories for this game someday

This is a bit unrealistic to how it would work if such a system worked in the real world. But these different changes do give you different outcomes potentially.

But obviously enjoying the game enough to restart it each time to see what happens :) I also wonder if you can purposey sabotage the system...choosing wrong information purposely. I may have to try it at some point.

Dig into the forums on this one before you purchase.  It's not quite the game description implies.   

As one person put it it's more of a "visual novel" where you play the untrusty narrator in an Orwellian future.  Great content and rich interface support that experience.   However if you're looking for the rabbit whole where you're investigating and shaping the lives of these "potential criminals" then this game misses that mark by not providing an organic sense of discovery to the player.  Most of the game is on rails, because it has to be, with so much content involved.

The creators put a lot of blood and treasure into this game and new content is coming out each week.  If you're looking to read a captivating story about a dark future ahead, then this game is for you (even more so after this week's election results).
